## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="m3-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Capacity expansion LP</dt><dd>Decides what to build (seven sizes, paid every year) and how to run it in every modelled hour, at least yearly cost.</dd>
<dt>Weights</dt><dd>Each modelled hour's running cost counts as many times as the hours of the year it stands for.</dd>
<dt>Extreme weeks</dt><dd>Peak demand, peak net load and least wind, kept as they were: they cut the full-year shortfall from 879 to 108 MWh.</dd>
<dt>Link between weeks</dt><dd>A calendar chain of 52 battery levels; without it, each week may start full for free.</dd>
<dt>Validation</dt><dd>Re-run the plan on every hour of 2025 and of 2024; report unserved energy, CO₂ against the cap and the estimate error.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The expansion LP in algebra</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For each representative week $p$ and hour $h = 1 \dots 168$, at least yearly cost:

$$\min \; \sum_i f_i K_i + \sum_p w_p \sum_{h} \big(r_\mathrm{cc}\, g_{p,h} + r_\mathrm{pk}\, q_{p,h}\big)$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
a^{w}_{p,h} K_\mathrm{wind} + a^{s}_{p,h} K_\mathrm{solar} + 0.911\,K_\mathrm{nuc} + g_{p,h} + q_{p,h} + d_{p,h} - c_{p,h} &\ge D_{p,h} && \text{(demand)}\\
g_{p,h} \le K_\mathrm{cc}, \quad q_{p,h} \le K_\mathrm{pk}, \quad c_{p,h} + d_{p,h} &\le K_\mathrm{bp} && \text{(sizes)}\\
s_{p,h} = s_{p,h-1} + 0.85\,c_{p,h} - d_{p,h}, \quad s_{p,0} = 0, \quad \ell_p \le s_{p,h} &\le u_p && \text{(battery, within week } p)\\
S_{i+1} = S_i + s_{k(i),168}, \quad S_{53} = S_1, \quad 0 \le S_i + \ell_{k(i)}, \quad S_i + u_{k(i)} &\le K_\mathrm{be} && \text{(link, calendar weeks } i)\\
\textstyle\sum_p w_p \sum_h \big(0.329\, g_{p,h} + 0.484\, q_{p,h}\big) &\le \text{cap} && \text{(CO}_2\text{)}\\
K_i,\ g_{p,h},\ q_{p,h},\ c_{p,h},\ d_{p,h},\ S_i \ge 0, \quad s_{p,h} \text{ free in sign}, \quad \ell_p \le 0 &\le u_p && \text{(domains)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Each step $h$ lasts one hour, so a power held for one step (MW) is that much energy (MWh). Sizes, outputs, charge and discharge cannot be negative; the level $s_{p,h}$ is measured from the week's start, so it can be.

The weight of a modelled hour: $w_p = n_p \times 8{,}760 / 8{,}736$, where $n_p$ is the number of calendar weeks it stands for and the factor spreads the 24 hours of 31 December. A typical week standing for 13 weeks: $13 \times 8{,}760 / 8{,}736 = 13.04$; an extreme week stands for itself.

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $K_i$ | size built; battery power $K_\mathrm{bp}$ | MW |
| $K_\mathrm{be}$ | battery energy | MWh |
| $f_i$ | yearly cost of one unit built: [capital recovery]{.lx-term term="capital-recovery-factor"} at 4% real plus [fixed O&M]{.lx-term term="fixed-om"}; for a plant with constant output, also its fuel and variable O&M | \$ per MW-year (per MWh-year) |
| $w_p$ | hours of the year one modelled hour of week $p$ stands for | h |
| $g, q$ | gas combined-cycle and peaker output | MW |
| $r_\mathrm{cc}, r_\mathrm{pk}$ | running cost of gas | \$/MWh |
| $c, d$ | battery charge and discharge | MW |
| $s_{p,h}$ | battery level in week $p$, relative to the week's start (may be negative) | MWh |
| $\ell_p, u_p$ | the lowest and highest $s_{p,h}$ in week $p$ | MWh |
| $S_i$ | battery level at the start of calendar week $i$; $k(i)$ is the representative week standing for it | MWh |
| $a^w, a^s$ | wind and solar output per MW built | MW per MW |
| $0.911$ | nuclear output per MW built, the same in every hour | MW per MW |
| $D$ | demand | MW |
| $0.329, 0.484$ | CO₂ per MWh of gas output ([heat rate]{.lx-term term="heat-rate"} × 0.05291 t per [MMBtu]{.lx-term term="mmbtu"}): operating CO₂ only | t/MWh |

Cyclic storage replaces the chain $S_{i+1} = S_i + s_{k(i),168}$ with $s_{p,168} = 0$ for every $p$: each week ends where it starts, from a start level of its own. No link drops the chain only: each week may start at any level, whatever the week before left. Fixing every $K_i$ and running all 8,760 hours as one period, with unserved demand allowed at an illustrative \$10,000 per MWh, gives the full-year check.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>How the weeks are chosen</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Typical weeks.** Each season's weeks (by the month of the week's middle) are grouped by k-medoids, $k$ = 1, 2 or 3. Each group's [medoid]{.lx-term term="medoid"} is the real week closest, hour by hour, to the others in its group: squared differences of demand (as a share of the peak), wind and solar output per MW.
- **Scaling.** A typical week is scaled so that its group keeps its demand energy, and its wind and solar energy to within 0.5%: no hour may exceed a plant's size.
- **Extremes.** The week of the year's peak demand, of the peak of demand minus reference wind and solar output, and of the least wind are kept as they were, each standing for itself.
- **Same weather year.** Demand, wind and sun come from the same hours, so their correlation survives.
- **Outages** are left out of the planning LP: they belong to an adequacy study.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Error measures, and what they cannot tell you</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

| Measure | Definition | 4 + 3 extreme weeks |
|---|---|---|
| Estimate error | (weeks' optimal cost) ÷ (full-year optimal cost) − 1 | −3.0% |
| Cost gap | (plan's spending on the full year) ÷ (weeks' estimate) − 1. Spending: plants and fuel; no shortage penalty, no cap in the re-run | +1.1% on 2025 |
| Unserved energy | demand not met when the plan is re-run, in MWh, hours and largest shortfall | 108 MWh in 8 hours |
| CO₂ against the cap | the plan's full-year CO₂ ÷ cap − 1 | +8.7% on 2025 (217 kt), +7.3% on 2024 (215 kt) |

- **Four typical weeks** leave 879 MWh unserved in 54 hours of 2025, spread over 12 weeks.
- **The second year.** At 2025's yearly demand energy, 2024's demand peaks at 462 MW, against 450 MW in 2025.
- **What they cannot tell you.** Even the plan optimal on all of 2025 leaves 235 MWh in 17 hours of 2024 unserved.
- **Adequacy** is judged over many weather years with plant outages, in a Monte Carlo study ([A5](a05-adequacy.qmd)), by measures such as the [loss-of-load expectation]{.lx-term term="lole"} (LOLE).
- **LOLE** is the expected number of days a year with a shortage of any size or length. One criterion is 0.1 days a year, “1 day in 10 years” ([PJM Manual 20A](https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m20a.pdf), §1.3, June 2026): an expectation, not a promise of one outage a decade.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this model leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Plant outages and reserve margins: adequacy studies treat them over many weather years (<a href="a05-adequacy.html">A5</a>).</li>
<li>Start-up costs and minimum run times: on/off decisions make a mixed-integer program (<a href="m02-unit-commitment.html">M2</a>).</li>
<li>Transmission and regions: the town is one bus with no imports.</li>
<li>Several years of investment, retirements and residual value: a pathway model (<a href="m13-national-pathway.html">M13</a>).</li>
<li>Uncertainty when building: here the weather is known when the sizes are chosen (<a href="m08-stochastic-robust.html">M8</a> chooses them before it is known).</li>
<li>Costs that change with time: every cost is constant within the year modelled.</li>
</ul>
<p>Modeler's note: <a href="r05-build-validate.html">R5</a> turns these checks into a verification and validation plan, and the Modeler checkpoint <a href="ck-m-unseen-problem.html">CK-M</a> asks you to formulate, solve and verify a model you have not seen.</p>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="m3-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="more" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “More representative weeks always give a better plan.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. 8 typical weeks leave 750 MWh unserved on the full year; 4 typical + 3 extreme leave 108 MWh. Which weeks matters as much as how many.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="link" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Leaving out the battery's link between weeks costs only a little accuracy.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In an illustrative what-if with storage energy at $20 per kWh (not a forecast or a sourced cost):</p>
<ul><li>the plan with no link builds 2,685 MWh of battery;</li><li>re-run on the full year, it emits 247 kt against a 200 kt cap;</li><li>each week could start charged, for free.</li></ul></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="adequate" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A plan that serves every hour of one full year is adequate.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. The plan optimized on all 8,760 hours of 2025 is short in 17 hours of 2024. Adequacy needs plant outages and many weather years.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="m3">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="err" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">The seven weeks estimate $129.28M a year; the full-year optimum costs $133.25M. What is the estimate error, as this lesson defines it?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">−3.0%</li><li data-value="b">+3.1%</li><li data-value="c">0.970</li><li data-value="d">−$3.97M</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>−3.0%: 129.28 ÷ 133.25 − 1 = −0.030, with the reference in the denominator. +3.1% reverses the comparison: the full-year optimum is 3.1% above the estimate (133.25 ÷ 129.28 − 1). 0.970 is the ratio before subtracting 1, and −$3.97M is the gap in dollars (129.28 − 133.25).</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>Open planning models offer the same choices. GenX's standard storage balance makes each representative period end where it starts; its long-duration storage option links the periods through the calendar, as in this lesson.</p>
<ul class="m3-links">
<li>Builds on: <a href="13-capstone.html">lesson 13</a> (the town's plan), <a href="09-storage.html">9</a> (state of charge) and <a href="m01-dispatch-to-lmp.html">M1</a> (an LP in full).</li>
<li>Open tools: <a href="https://genxproject.github.io/GenX.jl/">GenX</a>, <a href="https://docs.pypsa.org/">PyPSA</a> and NLR's <a href="https://www.nlr.gov/analysis/reeds/">ReEDS</a>.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
<ul>
<li>Kotzur, L., Markewitz, P., Robinius, M. and Stolten, D. (2018). <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2018.01.023">Time series aggregation for energy system design: Modeling seasonal storage</a>. Applied Energy 213, 123–135.</li>
<li>Hoffmann, M., Kotzur, L., Stolten, D. and Robinius, M. (2020). <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/en13030641">A Review on Time Series Aggregation Methods for Energy System Models</a>. Energies 13(3), 641.</li>
<li>GenX. <a href="https://genxproject.github.io/GenX.jl/stable/Model_Reference/Resources/long_duration_storage/">Long duration storage</a>: the standard storage balance and the inter-period link (documentation, accessed 3 Nov 2026).</li>
<li>EIA. <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">Hourly Electric Grid Monitor</a> (Form EIA-930): the Southwest Power Pool data for 2025 and 2024 (six-month files, accessed 3 Nov 2026).</li>
<li>Costs: EIA's Annual Energy Outlook 2026 assumptions (2025 dollars) and NREL's battery cost projections (2024 dollars, converted to 2025 dollars with BEA's GDP implicit price deflator), as listed in <a href="13-capstone.html#sources">lesson 13</a>.</li>
<li>PJM, Resource Adequacy Planning (2026). <a href="https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/documents/manuals/m20a.pdf">PJM Manual 20A: Resource Adequacy Analysis</a>, revision 3, effective 24 June 2026: §1.2 defines the loss-of-load expectation in days per year, §1.3 sets the criterion of 1 day in 10 years, or 0.1 days per year (p. 8; accessed 3 Nov 2026).</li>
<li>HiGHS. <a href="https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/">Documentation</a> of the open-source solver used in the page and, through SciPy, in the notebook.</li>
</ul>
</div>
```
